original.target_description: General recognition memory (similar/[1-same responses]), Delay × Valence interaction in the Sleep/Wake mixed ANOVA with object valence and scene component.

n.sample_role: Participants in the mutually exclusive wake-delay and sleep-delay groups entering the target general-recognition mixed ANOVA.
n.exclusions: Morning and evening 30-minute baseline groups (20 each) are outside this Sleep/Wake model. No participant exclusions or attrition reported in supplied Method or Results.
n.location: Method > Participants; Results > Sleep vs. wake, general-recognition mixed ANOVA
n.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: wake-delay condition (24 participants), sleep-delay condition (24 participants), morning 30-min condition (20 participants), or evening 30-min condition (20 participants). ... A 2 (Delay: Sleep, Wake) × 2 (Object valence: Negative, Neutral) × 2 (Scene component: Object, Background) mixed ANOVA revealed interactions between Delay and Valence,

notes: Independently checked source identity: canonical text is the PMC full author manuscript of Sleep Preferentially Enhances Memory for Emotional Components of Scenes, by Jessica D Payne, Robert Stickgold, Kelley Swanberg, and Elizabeth A Kensinger. Publication line Psychol Sci. 2008 Aug;19(8):781–788 and DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02157.x match the neutral original reference. Includes Method, Results, Discussion, and references, not merely an abstract. No PDF supplied; section locators used. Only assigned unfinished fields assessed; other fields are placeholders. Analytic N derivation: 24 wake-delay participants + 24 sleep-delay participants = 48 participants. Exclude morning and evening 30-minute baseline groups (20 + 20) from model scope; these are not attrition exclusions. The source assigns participants to one of four conditions; the target model explicitly compares Sleep and Wake. Printed F(1, 46) corroborates model scope; N is not derived from df. Target interaction identified by factors and outcome independently of row order. Other Analyses reports false-alarm-corrected versions of the same interactions with the same Sleep/Wake groups; that distinction does not affect assigned N.
